text: Giordano worked so fast that people nicknamed him Luca fa presto, which means Luca paints quickly. He trained with Ribera around 1650. His father Antonio was a painter, and Ribera's half length philosophers shaped Giordano, who painted many of them himself. Around 1652 he went to Rome for the first time and studied the Baroque art of Pietro da Cortona. He also earned the names The Thunderbolt and The Proteus of painting, since he could imitate other painters so well. Later he worked in Naples, Rome, Florence and Venice before ten years in Spain.

Italians nicknamed Honthorst Gherardo delle Notti, or Gerard of the Nights, for his scenes lit by artificial light. He was born in Utrecht, trained with his father, a decorative painter, and then with Abraham Bloemaert. In Rome he lodged at the palace of Vincenzo Giustiniani, where he painted Christ Before the High Priest. Cardinal Scipione Borghese became another patron. He came back to Utrecht in 1620. Queen Elizabeth of Bohemia, living in exile in the Netherlands, employed him as a painter and as a drawing master for her children, and through her Charles I invited him to England in 1628.

The Royal Danish Academy in Copenhagen turned Tidemand away at first. He studied at a private art school and soon became a pupil at the academy anyway. From 1837 he studied in Düsseldorf under Theodor Hildebrandt. In Hardanger he met the 18 year old Hans Gude, and the two became close friends who made landscape paintings together, with Tidemand adding the figures. He travelled around Norway to study folk costumes, tools and buildings. In 1848 King Oscar I asked him to paint a series of Norwegian peasant life for the palace of Oscarshall.

Macke lived most of his creative life in Bonn, with short stays at Lake Thun and trips to Paris, Italy, the Netherlands and Tunisia. His father was a building contractor and amateur artist, and his drawings were the first art to impress the boy. Macke enrolled at the Kunstakademie Düsseldorf in 1904, the year his father died. In Paris in 1907 he saw the Impressionists, and soon afterwards he spent a few months in Lovis Corinth's studio in Berlin. Through his friend Franz Marc he met Kandinsky. He died in the First World War.

Hackert's pictures of the Battle of Chesma were made for Catherine the Great, and some of his battle scenes hang in the Peterhof palace in Russia. He grew up in Prenzlau in Brandenburg, trained with his father, a portraitist and animal painter, and went to the Prussian Academy in Berlin. In Paris he worked mostly in gouache. He left for Italy in 1768 and settled mainly in Rome and Naples, where he produced many works for Sir William Hamilton. Goethe became his friend when he visited Naples in 1786. Goethe also wrote the first biography of Hackert.

Isabey drew himself and his family in a picture called Boat, and it was a success at the Salon of 1820. At 19 he became a pupil of Jacques-Louis David after lessons from the miniature painter François Dumont. He painted the dukes of Angoulême and Berry for the Palace of Versailles. Josephine and Napoleon Bonaparte both backed him, and he planned the ceremonies for their coronation and prepared drawings for the book that recorded it. Several rulers gave him commissions until his death in 1855. His son Eugène painted seascapes.

König made more than 100 transparent paintings, and he showed them by candlelight to paying audiences. He started in his father's trade as a decorative painter in Bern, then studied with Marquard Wocher and Sigmund Freudenberger and learned printmaking from Balthasar Anton Dunker. In 1797 the family left Bern for the Bernese Oberland, where he made coloured etchings, lithographs and small oil paintings for visitors. His costume pictures and scenes of country life came out as popular print series. In 1811 he began showing his Diaphanorama in Bern. Later he toured with it.

De Zwart's father painted carriages, and at 14 the boy was apprenticed to a carriage maker to learn the same trade. In his spare time he copied prints from magazines, and a year later he joined the evening class at the Royal Academy in The Hague. Maris took him into his studio. Jacob Maris once sent him to the coast without drawing materials and made him paint his impressions straight onto canvas when he got back. At the Mauritshuis he copied Vermeer, Potter and Rembrandt. People call him the Hague Breitner for his likeness to George Hendrik Breitner.

Hodges first made a living by painting theatre scenery, after he studied under William Shipley and in the studio of Richard Wilson. Between 1772 and 1775 he sailed with James Cook as the expedition's artist. The big oil paintings from that trip were finished in London, where the Admiralty paid him a salary to complete them. Critics complained that his strong light and colour contrasts made the pictures look rough and unfinished. In 1780 he went to India under the patronage of Warren Hastings. His Benares sketches later became the base for The Ghauts at Benares.

Houbraken says Visscher was an able etcher who had an unusual talent for drawing live models in charcoal. He was born and died in Haarlem, and he trained with Pieter Claesz Soutman. His prints copied painters from Haarlem such as Nicolaes Berchem, Adriaen van Ostade, Pieter van Laer and Adriaen Brouwer. He also made a series of portraits of religious figures from Amsterdam and Haarlem. In 1653 he joined the Haarlem Guild of St. Luke. His work influenced Dirk Helmbreker and Cornelis Bega.

Cort lived his last twelve years in Italy, where people called him Cornelio Fiammingo. He came from Hoorn or Edam, and his first known engravings came out in Antwerp around 1553, published by Hieronymus Cock. In 1565 he moved to Venice and lived in the house of Titian, and he engraved many of Titian's works. Later he went on to Bologna and Rome, and in Rome he founded a school of engraving. He may also have worked for the Medici in Florence. He is said to have engraved upwards of 151 plates.

Isabey wanted to be a sailor, but his father insisted that he study painting. After lessons with his father and copying at the Louvre, he shared a studio at Honfleur with the landscape painter Xavier Leprince in 1824. In 1831 he turned down a place on a diplomatic mission to Morocco, so his friend Delacroix went instead. Isabey became a court painter to King Louis-Philippe, and he painted the return of Napoleon's remains aboard the Belle Poule. He also painted many storms and shipwrecks. His students included Eugène Boudin and Johan Barthold Jongkind.

Verneuil took his ideas from Japanese art and from nature, especially the sea. He learned his trade from the Swiss designer Eugène Grasset. His bold floral designs went onto ceramic tiles, wallpapers and furnishing textiles, and he also made posters in France alongside artists such as Toulouse-Lautrec and Chéret. After the First World War he moved to Geneva. In 1923 he set off with his wife Adélaïde Verneuil de Marval, who was also a painter, on a long voyage to the Far East. He trained many artists, among them Amédée Ozenfant.

Mortimer's father was a customs officer who also dealt in flour and owned several mills. By 1757 the son was studying in London at the Duke of Richmond's Academy, where he became friends with Joseph Wright. In 1759 he won a first prize for a study after Michelangelo's Bacchus. The Society of Artists gave him prizes for paintings of British history, and he became its president in 1774. He painted the figures for several of Thomas Jones's landscapes. He died at 39.

Modersohn-Becker painted many self-portraits, some of them nudes. She grew up in Dresden as the third of seven children, and her father worked as an engineer for the German railway. In 1888 the family moved to Bremen. She is recognised as the first known woman painter to paint nude self-portraits, and she is believed to be the first woman artist to show herself pregnant. A museum devoted only to her work opened in 1927. She died at 31.

Decamps showed everyday life in the East to Paris at the Salon of 1831. In his youth he travelled there and painted Oriental life and scenery with a bold truth to nature that puzzled conventional critics. Before long he was ranked with Delacroix and Ingres as one of the leaders of the French school. His brushstrokes were bold and sometimes rough, and his colour and light had startling contrasts. He also painted Bible scenes against a true local background. He loved dogs and field sports, and in 1860 he died after a fall from a horse while hunting at Fontainebleau.

Chodowiecki made several thousand etchings, mostly small ones, and they show the life of the middle classes in great detail. He grew up in Danzig, and his father died when Daniel was 16, so the two brothers went to live with an uncle in Berlin. In Augsburg a painter named Haid gave him his art training. He was admitted to the Berlin Academy in 1764 and became its director in 1797. Much of his work was illustrating books, among them scientific books by Basedow, Buffon, Lavater and Pestalozzi. He died in 1801.

Burger and his old friend Jakob Fürchtegott Dielmann founded the Kronberg Artists' Colony in 1861, and he stayed there until he died. People called him the King of Kronberg. He had studied at the Städelschule in Frankfurt, where Philipp Veit told him to go to Munich. A study trip to Paris brought him together with Corot and Courbet. After he moved to Kronberg, a visit to Antwerp and Amsterdam left him deeply influenced by the Old Masters. In the region around Kronberg, owning a Burger showed good taste.

Dawe painted 329 portraits of Russian generals who fought during Napoleon's invasion, for the Military Gallery of the Winter Palace. He moved to Saint Petersburg in 1819. Pushkin wrote friendly verses about him. His father Philip was a mezzotint engraver, and George first trained with him as an engraver before he turned to painting and won the gold medal of the Royal Academy Schools in 1803. He carried out dissections in his own home to understand the human body better. Classical pictures made his early name, but he cared more about money and went after portrait commissions.

Boys was articled to the engraver George Cooke. When that ended he went to Paris, where Richard Parkes Bonington talked him out of engraving and into painting. William Callow later shared a studio with him there. He stayed in Paris until 1837 and then went home to lithograph the works of David Roberts and Clarkson Stanfield. His collection of colour lithographs, Picturesque Architecture in Paris, Ghent, Antwerp, Rouen, etc., appeared in 1839, and King Louis-Philippe sent him a ring. He also etched some plates for John Ruskin's Stones of Venice.

Gottlob's 1900 poster for the second exhibition of painter lithographers on the Rue Drouot in Paris shows a strong influence of Toulouse-Lautrec. He studied under the painter and decorator Armand Jobbé-Duval, and his work began to appear in the official salons in 1891. His caricatures ran in Le Rire, Le Sourire and other humorous magazines. In 1904 he joined the Cornet Society, and he designed twelve menus for it. Besides prints and portraits, he painted cityscapes of Paris and landscapes of Normandy and Brittany.

Goodwin & Company began as E. Goodwin and Brother, a New York tobacco firm founded before the American Civil War. Its cigarette brands were Gypsy Queen and Old Judge. In 1887 it was among the first to issue trading cards to promote its brands, at first as sepia photographic prints. Its Old Judge set, made from 1887 to 1890, held over 2,000 images and was the first major set of baseball cards. The 1888 Goodwin Champions set showed 50 athletes and was the firm's first set printed in colour. The firm then merged into James Buchanan Duke's American Tobacco Company.

Forbes studied under Arthur Fitzwilliam Tait and started out as an animal and landscape painter. During the Civil War he was a special artist for Frank Leslie's Magazine, and he drew detailed, dramatic sketches of soldiers and battles. General Sherman later gave many of his etchings to the government, and they are kept in the War Office at Washington. After the war Forbes painted landscapes and cattle scenes. In 1877 he became an honorary member of the London Etching Club. He died in Brooklyn.

Krøyer was raised in Copenhagen by his aunt and her husband, the zoologist Henrik Nikolai Krøyer, after his mother was judged unfit to care for him. He showed talent at nine and enrolled at the Royal Danish Academy at twelve. In 1874 Heinrich Hirschsprung bought four of his watercolours of fishermen, and that began a lifelong friendship and patronage. Three years later a travel scholarship took him around Europe for years. In Paris he studied under Léon Bonnat and came under the influence of Impressionists such as Monet and Degas. He was one of the Skagen Painters.

Díaz lost his leg as a boy, after a reptile bit his foot in a wood near Sèvres, and the wooden stump that replaced it became famous. He was an orphan at ten. At fifteen he entered the studios at Sèvres, where he decorated porcelain before he turned to painting. Around 1831 he met Théodore Rousseau at Fontainebleau and admired him. Once he followed Rousseau into the forest on his wooden leg to watch how he worked, and in the end Rousseau taught him everything he knew. In 1851 Díaz became a Chevalier of the Légion d'honneur.

Moras was called a Berlin painter all his life, yet he scarcely painted in Berlin itself. He trained in the Berlin studio of the landscape painter Hermann Eschke, and in 1876 he held his first exhibition at the Prussian Academy of Arts. On Eschke's advice he painted in Mecklenburg and on the island of Rügen. Many of his pictures came from rural Brandenburg and later the Spreewald. His style was realistic, with a touch of melancholy. He became known for winter landscapes and for large autumn scenes in warm colours, and his son Bruno also became a painter.

Haskell expected to go to Yale on a football scholarship, but his drawing caught people's eye and led to an offer of work in magazine illustration. He mostly taught himself, and over the next ten years he made three long trips to Paris, where he joined the Académie Julian but did not stay. For a time he was a protege and friend of Whistler, who taught him to etch. He also made posters for magazines such as Scribner's and Collier's. In the First World War the army asked him to develop camouflage.

Van der Borcht brought a new subject into northern art, the monkey scene, also called a singerie. He came from Mechelen, and by 1564 he was working from there for the Antwerp printer Christopher Plantin. He made the drawings for the engravings in many scientific books, including those of Rembert Dodoens and Carolus Clusius. In 1572 Spanish troops sacked Mechelen, and the family fled to Antwerp with almost nothing. Plantin took them in. Van der Borcht stayed in Antwerp as Plantin's full time assistant and illustrated many liturgical books for the Spanish market.

Cicéri came from an artistic family. His father was the stage designer Pierre-Luc-Charles Cicéri, his grandfather was the painter Jean-Baptiste Isabey, and his uncle was Eugène Isabey, who gave him his first lessons along with his father. He was one of the first artists to work in Bourron-Marlotte, where he settled in 1849. Two years later he showed at the Salon for the first time. He also published albums of lithographs based on photographs, among them views of the Pyrenees, Switzerland and Savoy. Like his father, he designed theatre sets.

Puvis de Chavannes was born Pierre-Cécile Puvis, the son of a mining engineer, and he added the old family name de Chavannes later. He meant to follow his father's profession until a serious illness stopped his studies. After a trip to Italy he told his family in 1846 that he would be a painter. He studied briefly under Delacroix, who soon closed his studio, and then under Henri Scheffer and Thomas Couture. He preferred to work alone, and his training was not classical. Zola described his work as an art made of reason, passion and will.

In 1894 Picabia copied a collection of Spanish paintings that belonged to his grandfather, swapped the copies for the originals and sold the originals to pay for his stamp collection. His mother died of tuberculosis when he was five, and his father raised him. Three years after the swindle he eloped to Switzerland with one of his mistresses. He tried Impressionism and Pointillism, then Cubism, and he became an early figure of Dada in the United States and France. He denounced Dada in 1921. Later he was briefly linked with Surrealism.

Waldmüller attended the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna as a young man. He married the singer Katharina Weidner and went on tour with her as a set designer. Back in Vienna, he copied old masters and painted portraits, among them one of Beethoven in 1823. Later he turned to landscapes, painted with loving attention to detail, because he believed the close study of nature should be the base of painting. That brought him into disputes with the academy. He was forced to retire in 1857, and Vienna took him back by 1863.

Modersohn made his first visit to Worpswede in July 1889 with Fritz Mackensen, and other students from Düsseldorf followed. In 1895 the group held its first show at the Kunsthalle Bremen, and critics mostly panned it. His first wife died after a long illness, and he later married Paula Becker, who was also a painter. She died in 1907 of an embolism, shortly after the birth of their daughter. He then moved to nearby Fischerhude. He was the only Worpswede artist to support the Kunsthalle Bremen when it bought Van Gogh's Field with Poppies.

Rousseau was known as le grand refusé, the great refused one, because the Salon jury kept turning him down. In 1836 his large Paysage du Jura was rejected. Eight more works sent between 1836 and 1841 were refused too. After that he sent nothing until 1849, when all three of his entries were accepted. His friend, the critic Théophile Thoré, spoke up for him in the press. His father first regretted that he gave up business for painting, but later backed him in every fight with the Salon.

Vorsterman joined the workshop of Rubens around 1618 and soon became his only engraver. In 1621 a violent dispute broke out, and Rubens's lawyers asked the authorities for a protection order. The cause is not known, but most think it was a fight over who owned the rights to the prints, although Rubens had been godfather to his eldest son. In 1624 Vorsterman went to England and lived on the support of royalty and nobles. Back in Antwerp, he engraved twenty-two of the eighty plates for Van Dyck's Iconography. Old age brought blindness and poverty.

Smits paid 2,000 Belgian francs for a small farm in Achterbos near Mol and built it up into his Malvinahof. He was born in Rotterdam, the son of a decorator, and later studied in Brussels and Munich. A friendship with the painter Albert Neuhuys led to trips together to Drenthe and the Campine in Belgium. The Campine landscape moved him, and in 1888 he settled in Achterbos for good. He lived in poverty there. In 1901 he held his first one man show in Antwerp, and critics praised it, but he found no buyers.

Koryūsai started out as a samurai in the service of the Tsuchiya clan. When the head of the clan died, he became a masterless rōnin and moved to Edo, where he settled near Ryōgoku Bridge. In 1769 he became a print designer under the art name Haruhiro, at first with samurai themes. After Harunobu died in 1770, he began making prints in a similar style of life in the pleasure districts. He made about 2,500 known designs. One series of beauties ran for 140 prints, the longest known in ukiyo-e.

Leighton had family money behind him. His grandfather was the physician to two Russian tsars, and his father paid him an allowance all his life. He trained in Europe, first with Eduard von Steinle and then with Giovanni Costa. At 17 he met the philosopher Arthur Schopenhauer in Frankfurt and drew his portrait, the only known full length study of Schopenhauer done from life. From 1855 he lived in Paris for four years and met Ingres, Delacroix, Corot and Millet. His peerage was the shortest in history, because it ended with his death after one day.

Born Pieter van der Faes in Soest, where his father served as an officer, Lely is said to have taken his new name from a lily on the gable of a house in The Hague. He studied in Haarlem and became a master of the guild there in 1637. He arrived in London around 1643. After Anthony van Dyck's death he became the most fashionable portrait painter in England. His career survived Charles I's execution, and he painted Oliver Cromwell warts and all. In 1661 Charles II named him his Principal Painter in Ordinary.

Claude came from the Duchy of Lorraine, but he spent most of his life in Italy. He is one of the earliest artists in the west to concentrate on landscape. He often added a few small figures to a landscape, so that it passed as a history painting of a Bible or classical scene. He brought the sun and streaming sunlight into many paintings, which had been rare before. Over time his landscapes grew larger, with fewer figures, and he painted them more carefully and at a slower rate. English collectors loved his work after his death.

Roghman was the son of an engraver, his mother came from the Savery family, and he studied with his great uncle and namesake, Roelant Savery. Houbraken says he had only one eye but still painted in a rough and ready way. He specialized in landscapes, and he followed Rembrandt and Hercules Seghers. With his sister Geertruydt he worked on a series of more than 200 prints of castles and country estates in North Holland and Utrecht, which proved very popular. He never married and died in the old men's almshouse in Amsterdam.

Quellinus came from a family of sculptors and painters, and his brother was the sculptor Artus Quellinus the Elder. His engravings after Artus helped spread the Flemish Baroque style across Europe. In 1650 he went to Rome and joined the Bentvueghels. His nickname there was Saracin. By 1660 he was in Amsterdam, working on a publication about the new City Hall, and six years later he sold Frederik de Wit 113 copper plates for it, with the 15 year patent. He was mainly an engraver of architecture.

Simpson grew up poor in Glasgow, with a father who was a shipyard labourer. At fourteen he was an apprentice in a lithographic firm, and later he was bound for seven years to another one. In his time off he sketched from nature. He left for London in 1851 and took a job with the lithographers Day and Son. When the Crimean War began, the firm Colnaghi asked him to go to the Crimea and sketch for them. He was struck by the plight of the common soldiers and became a special artist for the Illustrated London News.

Ward's career splits into two parts. Until 1803 his greatest influence was his brother in law, George Morland, and after that it was Rubens. Later he specialised in painting horses in landscapes, and a little after that he turned to very large landscapes, among them Gordale Scar, finished around 1814, which shows a Yorkshire gorge as an example of the sublime. He gave much of the next six years to a gigantic Allegory of Waterloo, now lost. It earned little praise and little money. Like many artists then, he took commissions from gentry for their favourite horses and hunting dogs.

Ostoja-Chrostowski studied painting with Tadeusz Pruszkowski and woodcut with Władysław Skoczylas at the School of Fine Arts in Warsaw. Commercial art he learned from Edmund Bartłomiejczyk. In 1936 he won a bronze medal in the art competitions of the Olympic Games for a yachting club certificate. During the Second World War he worked in the intelligence department of the underground Polish Home Army. After the war he was elected rector of the rebuilt Academy of Fine Arts in Warsaw. His daughter Halina Chrostowska became an artist too.

Bauer used photographs he bought on his travels as the base for many of his works. His father was a stage painter who encouraged his early drawing. At the Royal Academy in The Hague he found the teaching too conservative and left without graduating. In 1888 the dealer Van Wisselingh paid for a study trip to Istanbul, and Bauer decided to make Orientalism his main subject. He later travelled to North Africa and India, and as far as the Dutch East Indies, sketching and collecting items for the firm. In 1902 he married the painter Jo Stumpff.

Lathrop's father was the American consul to Hawaii, and the boy came into the world on a ship off the islands. He studied with T. C. Farrer in New York and then in Dresden, until Whistler invited him to London. Money trouble sent him home for a year, but he rejoined Whistler. In 1870 he left for Ford Madox Brown and Burne-Jones, and he studied stained glass in William Morris's school. Back in New York in 1873, he taught painting at Cooper Institute and designed the chancel of Trinity Church in Boston. His Marquand Memorial Window burned in 1922.

Guercino got his nickname, which means the squinter, because he was cross-eyed. He came from a family of peasant farmers in Cento and was mainly self-taught. At 16 he worked as an apprentice in the shop of the painter Benedetto Gennari. Between 1615 and 1616 he painted frescoes for Casa Pannini in Cento, where his landscapes already show real independence. In Bologna Ludovico Carracci praised him. His painting Et in Arcadia ego, from around 1618, holds the first known use of that Latin motto.

Leclerc once quit a job as engineer and geographer to a marshal when he heard that the king had passed off one of his drawings as another artist's work. He was born in Metz, the son of a goldsmith, and went to Paris in 1665 to study military engineering. Charles Le Brun saw some of his engravings and told him to drop the sciences and devote himself to engraving. In 1672 he joined the Académie Royale and taught perspective there. He worked for Louis XIV as graveur du Roi. He and his wife had six sons and four daughters.

Lyon was where Pillement began and ended his life, but he led an unusually cosmopolitan career. At 15 he went to Paris to work as an apprentice designer for Jean-Baptiste Oudry. In 1745 he left for Madrid and stayed five years, and then he moved to Lisbon, where he turned down an offer to become court painter. He spent eight years in England, and then Vienna and Warsaw employed him. Later he made decorations for Marie Antoinette at the Petit Trianon. Engravings after his drawings helped spread the Rococo style and the taste for chinoiserie across Europe.

West said his mother's kiss made him a painter. As a child he had painted his little sister's portrait with ink from some bottles, and his mother kissed him when she saw it. He was the tenth child of an innkeeper, and he was entirely self-taught. In 1756 a gunsmith named William Henry, who was his patron, urged him to paint a Death of Socrates. West later toured Europe and settled in London, where he became historical painter to King George III. He was also the second president of the Royal Academy, after Reynolds.

Bracquemond never had formal art training, though she got limited lessons from Ingres and advice from Gauguin. She showed work at the Paris Salon while still an adolescent. She married the printmaker Félix Bracquemond, and together they made ceramic art for Haviland. Their son said his father was jealous of her work and refused to show her paintings to visitors. She took part in three of the eight Impressionist exhibitions, in 1879, 1880 and 1889. Only 31 of her at least 157 works have been found.

Tissot's father was a drapery merchant and his mother a milliner who designed hats, and people believe this shaped the fine detail he later gave to women's clothing. By 17 he knew he wanted to paint. His father opposed it, but his mother backed him. He moved to London in 1871 and began a relationship with Kathleen Newton, who lived with him until her death in 1882. For Vanity Fair he drew caricatures under the pseudonym Coïdé. He stayed close to the Impressionists, among them Whistler and Degas.

Copley's mother ran a tobacco shop on Long Wharf in Boston, and a family story says he could draw well as a child. He became a portrait painter of the wealthy in colonial New England. In 1774 he moved to London and never went back to America. There he painted large history pictures that were new in showing modern subjects in modern dress. He also met success as a portraitist for about twenty years. His later years went worse, and he died deep in debt.

Scholderer went to the Städel academy in Frankfurt for two years and then worked there as a freelance painter. His friend Victor Müller showed him the work of Courbet, and later Müller married his sister. On short study trips to Paris he became friends with Fantin-Latour and Manet. Fantin-Latour painted him in Studio aux Batignolles. From 1858 he lived mostly in Kronberg, close to the painters' colony there, and in 1871 he went to London, where he married his wife Luise. He returned to Frankfurt and died there in 1902.

Sandby followed his brother Thomas in 1745 into the military drawing department at the Tower of London, where the job included designs for bridges and fortifications. In Scotland he made watercolour landscapes of the land after the rebellion. He later stayed with his brother at Windsor and drew the castle and the town, and Sir Joseph Banks bought those drawings. Gainsborough said that for real views from nature there was no better artist than Sandby. He was a founding member of the Royal Academy in 1768. In 1760 he issued twelve etchings of The Cries of London.

Greive was the son of a musician, and he learned from his uncle Petrus Franciscus Greive and from Cornelis Springer. He signed his works J.C. Greive jr., and from 1863 he belonged to Arti et Amicitiae, where he served as chairman for three years. His pupils were Coen Metzelaar and Hein Kever. He painted, made lithographs and filled sketchbooks with topographical drawings, many of Amsterdam. A street in Amsterdam is named after him. A record price for his work was paid in 2013, for Seine near Châtillon.

De Gheyn got his first training in Antwerp from his father, who worked as a glass painter and engraver. In 1585 he moved to Haarlem and studied under Hendrik Goltzius for five years. His first commission came from Prince Maurice of Orange, for an engraving of the Siege of Geertruidenberg. Around 1600 he gave up engraving for painting and etching. In 1605 he moved to The Hague and designed a garden for the prince that had the first two grottoes in the Netherlands. He made some of the earliest female nudes, vanitas pictures and flower still lifes in Dutch art.

John Ruskin once examined Meissonier's work at length under a magnifying glass and marvelled at his skill with fine detail. His father owned a dye factory and expected him to join the business. At seventeen he got leave to become an artist. He painted Napoleon and military sieges, but also scenes of chivalry and adventure in earlier French life, and his work commanded enormous prices. In 1846 he bought a great mansion in Poissy with two large studios. He was one of the three most successful artists of the Second Empire, along with Gérôme and Cabanel.

Nooms was also called Zeeman, the Dutch word for sailor, and he started painting and drawing in 1643 after a rough and drunken life at sea. Nobody knows how he learned his skill. His ships and foreign places are accurate and highly detailed, and other artists used them as examples. Dutch victories in the Anglo-Dutch Wars were a favourite subject, and in 1661 he sailed along the North African coast with Michiel de Ruyter. In the 1650s he made a series of etchings of ships and views. One of his last works, from 1664, shows the Amsterdam harbour.

A student and adopted son of Tsukioka Yoshitoshi, Kōgyo also studied with Ogata Gekkō. Though he sometimes painted other subjects, for most of his career he made pictures of Japanese Noh theatre. They were large paintings or coloured woodblock prints. Many of the prints came out in series and were sold as multi volume sets. Some sets, such as Nōgaku zue, survive as albums in their original bindings. Most of the bound sets belong to institutions, but individual prints still turn up with dealers who specialise in Japanese prints.

At fifteen Davies saw a touring show of American landscape art in his hometown of Utica, with works by George Inness and the Hudson River School, and it had a deep effect on him. Inness's tonalist landscapes impressed him most. His family moved to Chicago, where he studied at the Chicago Academy of Design from 1879 to 1882. Then he went to New York and the Art Students League. He worked as a magazine illustrator before he gave himself to painting. In 1892 he married Virginia Meriwether, one of the first female physicians in New York State.

In 1800 Hamilton Smith ran an experiment on which colour should be used for military uniforms. He tested how well a rifle company shot at grey, green and red targets, and he showed that grey, and to a lesser extent green, gave the better cover. The army did not listen. His career began in 1787, when he studied at an Austrian academy for artillery and engineers in Flanders. He taught himself to draw, and he wrote and illustrated Costume of the Army of the British Empire. He estimated that he had made over 38,000 drawings.

Bernard grew up partly with his grandmother in Lille, who owned a laundry with more than twenty workers and strongly backed his art. The family moved to Paris in 1878. In 1884 he joined the Atelier Cormon, where he made friends with Louis Anquetin and Toulouse-Lautrec. After he was suspended for showing expressive tendencies in his paintings, he toured Brittany on foot. In 1886 he met Gauguin in Pont-Aven, and he also wrote plays, poetry and art criticism. Most of his notable painting came while he was still young.

Daniell began as an apprentice to a heraldic painter and later worked for a coach painter. He showed 30 works at the Royal Academy, mainly landscapes, but he found it hard to make his name in Britain. In 1784 he got permission from the East India Company to go to Calcutta as an engraver, with his nephew William as his assistant. They reached the city in 1786. He then made a set of twelve views of Calcutta, and he wrote that he had to stand Painter, Engraver, Copper-smith, Printer and Printer's Devil himself. He spent seven years in India.

Mueller trained as a lithographer in Görlitz and Breslau and then studied at the academy in Dresden. He left the academy in Munich after Franz von Stuck called him untalented. He destroyed many of his early works himself. When he settled in Berlin in 1908 his style became more expressionist, and in 1910 he joined Die Brücke, the Dresden group of Expressionist artists. After the war he taught at the academy in Breslau until his death. In 1937 the Nazis seized 357 of his works from German museums as degenerate art.

Chauveau left nearly 1,600 works, such as frontispieces and vignettes. He came from an impoverished noble family and studied in the studio of Laurent de La Hyre, where he specialised in etching. He engraved the Map of Tendre and the frontispiece for Mademoiselle de Scudéry's Artamène, and he also illustrated works by Scarron, Molière, Racine and Boileau. La Fontaine summoned him to illustrate the first six books of his fables. In 1662 Louis XIV gave him a pension and the title Graveur du Roi. He was the first printmaker to join the Académie royale, in 1663.

Richards worked as a designer and illustrator of ornamental metalwork while he studied part time with the German artist Paul Weber. His first public show was in New Bedford in 1858, organized by Albert Bierstadt. In 1866 he went to Europe for a year. He turned away from the romantic, stylized approach of other Hudson River painters and insisted on exact, factual renderings, so his views of the White Mountains look almost like photographs. In later years he painted almost only marine watercolours. He built a house in Jamestown, Rhode Island, and lived there for the rest of his life.

Schouman kept a detailed diary of his professional life, which was unusual among painters, from 1733 to 1753. At 15 he was an apprentice to Adriaan van der Burg in Dordrecht, alongside Cornelis Greenwood, whose father Frans taught Schouman glass engraving. From 1742 he headed the Dordrecht Guild of St. Luke. He travelled to England twice and put together a collection of paintings. He designed tapestries and decorated fans, snuffboxes and even the glass windows of a magic lantern. He died in The Hague at 82.

Wierink trained as a teacher but went to work as a draughtsman in the office of the architect P.J.H. Cuypers, where he helped with the plans for the new Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam. Later he taught drawing for forty years at a teacher training college and was director of the Industrieschool from 1888 to 1929. He was among the first Dutch artists of his time to make picture books for children from artistic principles. His books include Pim's poppetjes and Jan Klaassen. In 1908 he published a drawing method for primary schools called Geen dag zonder lijn.

Last began drawing on stone in 1824 for the publisher Portman in Amsterdam. In 1828 the Belgian Deguerrois asked him to help with a large painting, and for that he learned lithography from Jean-Baptiste Madou and moved to The Hague. There he did well as a painter and above all as a lithographer. He took part in many albums of animal studies, city views and landscapes. He also made single sheets and book illustrations, mostly after the designs of others. In 1853 he made a lithograph of the reception of King William III at the town hall of Zaandam.

Marcus came from the West Indies, born on Sint Eustatius, and moved to Amsterdam in 1783 with his father, who died the next year. A merchant, Balthazar Ortt, became his guardian. He had drawing lessons from Steven Goblé and learned engraving from Reinier Vinkeles. In 1798 he won the gold medal of the city drawing academy. He painted, but he became known mainly as a printmaker who made etchings, engravings and lithographs after artists such as Jacob Cats and Jan Steen. In 1820 he became teaching director of the Royal Academy of Fine Arts.

Zampis worked full time as an official at the imperial court treasury in Vienna from 1841, and as an artist he was self taught. He published humorous and satirical scenes of everyday Viennese life, with laundry girls, cab drivers and lamplighters. Horses were also among his favourite subjects. He became known for his political caricatures during the revolution of 1848, and he made fun of the interior minister Franz von Pillersdorf. In 1873 he tried running a bureau that found rooms for visitors to the Vienna world fair. He died poor at 63.

Little is known about the life of Nolpe. Some authors say he was born in The Hague in 1601, but even his birth date and place are not certain. No work of his as a painter is known, only as an engraver and etcher. He made prints of history scenes, portraits and landscapes, often of his own invention, and others after Rubens and Berchem. His best known print is probably the Bursting of St. Anthony's Dike. He worked mostly in Amsterdam from 1633 until his death.

Stopendaal was probably trained as a printmaker and draughtsman by his father, Bastiaan Stopendael, who had the same trade. Between 1685 and 1713 he worked in Amsterdam. He made engravings and etchings of maps and world maps, and some of his maps appeared in a Bible printed in Dordrecht. He also drew and etched many well known town houses and country estates for rich people in Amsterdam. A book with dozens of his copper engravings, De zegepraalende Vecht, came out in 1719.

Brandes worked as a Lutheran pastor in Doetinchem and drew on the side, and in 1778 the Lutheran church in Batavia called him there. His wife died in Batavia less than a year after they arrived. In the East he made a great many drawings and watercolours, of plants and animals and of scenes from his own daily life that nobody else recorded. On the way home he visited Ceylon and lived a year at the Cape. In 1789 he bought an estate in Sweden with the money he had earned in Batavia.

Bernigeroth trained in the workshop of his father, the engraver Martin Bernigeroth, in Leipzig, and he later took it over with his brother Johann Benedikt. Following French models, he refined his technique in showing ornament and fabrics. He made many portraits and book vignettes. He turned down a call to Saint Petersburg and was given the title of court engraver instead. During the Seven Years' War he anonymously engraved 80 battle plans, and in 1763 he published them together as Neues Kriegs-Theater. His son Martin Friedrich also became an engraver.

Schelfhout's grandfather was the landscape painter Andreas Schelfhout, and his father was an opera singer. After art school in Haarlem he had to earn his own living, and in 1900 he moved to Lüdenscheid as a painter and piano teacher. Later he lived among the artists around the Café du Dôme in Montparnasse. There he took Cézanne and Van Gogh as models and then Cubism, under the influence of Henri Le Fauconnier. In 1911 Piet Mondrian moved in with him and the painter Conrad Kickert. In 1913 he went home as the first Dutch Cubist.

MacLaughlan left Boston for Paris at twenty and studied with Gérôme and Jean-Paul Laurens at the École des Beaux-Arts. Four years later he had grown close to Whistler and learned from Rembrandt, so he gave up painting for etching. Most of his plates show views of Paris. In 1908 Alfred Stieglitz was impressed by his work and showed it at the 291 Gallery in New York. He made more than 300 plates. In 1938 he was elected to the National Academy of Design, and he died soon afterwards in Marrakech.

Monticelli grew up in humble circumstances in Marseille and later studied in Paris under Paul Delaroche, copying the Old Masters in the Louvre and admiring the oil sketches of Delacroix. In 1855 he met Narcisse Diaz, and the two often painted together in the Fontainebleau Forest. His style was highly personal, with richly coloured, dappled and glazed surfaces. After 1870 he returned to Marseille and lived in poverty, although he painted a great deal. He once said, "I paint for thirty years from now." Van Gogh admired his work.

As a child prodigy Kauffman quickly learned four languages from her mother. Her father was a muralist and trained her, and she worked as his assistant. She was also a skilled singer, but a priest told her that opera was a dangerous place, and she chose art. By twelve she was known as a painter, and bishops and nobles sat for her. In 1762 she was elected to the Accademia delle Arti del Disegno in Florence. She was one of two women among the founding members of the Royal Academy in London in 1768.

Nieuwenkamp was mainly self taught, and he worked mostly in ink, with drawings in rich sepia tones. In 1900 he built a houseboat called De Zwerver, The Wanderer, which was also his own nickname, and sailed it through the Netherlands, Belgium and Germany to hold exhibitions on board. He was one of the first European artists to visit Bali. After the Dutch military attack of 1906 he painted the ruins of Denpasar, and the drawing appeared in his book Bali and Lombok. Bali made a deep impact on him. He kept going back.

Schmid learned the basics of drawing and painting in Lucerne and later in the painters' colony of Johann Heinrich Bleuler in Feuerthalen. In Zürich he worked as a colourist of costume pictures for art dealers. He is much better known for his views of the landscapes of central and eastern Switzerland. Like his brothers Franz and Martin, he sold many gouaches and drawings to wealthy tourists. For his panoramas he chose especially picturesque spots and added country figures to give them an Arcadian look. His dramatic pictures of the Goldau landslide are well known.

Huret began engraving young in Lyon, a major centre of printing. In 1635 he went to Paris and settled in the rue Saint-Jacques. In 1663 he was admitted to the Académie royale de peinture et de sculpture as its fourth engraver, and the following year he gave it his Théâtre de la Passion de Notre Seigneur Jésus Christ. His prints number close to 500. In his last years he turned to more personal projects. His treatise Optique de portraiture et de peinture, published in 1670, challenged the perspective method of Abraham Bosse.

Bolswert came from the little town of Bolsward in Friesland and moved early to Holland, where he lived in Amsterdam and sometimes in Utrecht. In 1610 he made four scenes of the Horrors of the Spanish War after designs by David Vinckboons. He worked closely with Abraham Bloemaert and copied his graphic style. Their work on saints and hermits ended in 1619 in the Sylva Anachoretica, a volume of imaginary portraits of 25 male and 25 female hermits of antiquity. He was also the elder brother and teacher of the engraver Schelte à Bolswert.

Schut was active in Amsterdam from 1631 to 1660. In 1631 he worked for Balthasar Florisz van Berckenrode, and from 1635 he worked with Claes Jansz Visscher. He specialised in religious subjects and in topographical views. He made devotional prints and views of the main European cities, mostly in Flanders and Amsterdam. His prints include the departure of Charles II from the Netherlands for England, a portrait of Kenau Simonsdochter Hasselaer and a view of the Dam in Amsterdam.

The Strobridge Lithographing Company began in 1847 in Cincinnati as a stationery store, and it took its name from Hines Strobridge, who joined it later. Strobridge became sole owner after the American Civil War. In 1884 he built the company's first factory on the Miami and Erie Canal. Its lithographs became a popular way to advertise circuses and theaters, with designs by artists such as Mucha. The Cincinnati artist Harry Loud Bridwell made many of its calendar cards. From 1909 the firm also printed Christmas Seals for the American Tuberculosis Association.

Washington Duke started his first tobacco company, W. Duke and Sons, in 1865 in a converted corn crib. With his sons Ben and Buck he made pipe tobacco under the brand name Pro Bono Publico, between 400 and 500 pounds a day. The firm later went by the name W. Duke, Sons & Co. It issued small picture cards, such as its Miniature Novelties series, to promote Honest Long Cut Tobacco. In 1890 the company was merged with others to form the American Tobacco Company.

Skoczylas gave up oil painting for watercolours because of an allergy that gave him a rash on his hands. His father was a foreman in the salt mines. At the Kraków Academy of Fine Arts he studied painting with Teodor Axentowicz and Leon Wyczółkowski, and sculpture with Konstanty Laszczka. From 1910 he studied sculpture in Paris with Antoine Bourdelle, and then he took woodcut classes in Leipzig. In 1922 he got the chair of graphics at the School of Fine Art in Warsaw. At the 1928 Olympics he won a bronze medal for watercolours on the subject of archery.

Lawrence's father kept an inn in Devizes, and he greeted guests by offering to have his young son recite poetry or draw their portraits. By the age of ten, living in Bath, the boy supported his family with pastel portraits. At 18 he went to London, where his first royal commission, a portrait of Queen Charlotte, came in 1789. He taught himself and became president of the Royal Academy in 1820. Later the Prince Regent sent him abroad to paint allied leaders for the Waterloo Chamber at Windsor Castle. He never married, and he was deep in debt.
